segments.text: God made the heavens and the earth, then planted a beautiful garden called Eden. He placed Adam there to tend it and enjoy its trees.
God breathed life into Adam. Every creature had a place, but Adam needed a companion.
God made Eve from Adam's side and brought her to him. They belonged together, unashamed and at peace.
God gave them the garden's fruit, but one tree was forbidden: the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. He warned them not to eat it.
A serpent spoke to Eve and questioned God's command. It promised that the forbidden fruit would make them like God, knowing good and evil.
Eve saw that the fruit looked good, took it, and ate. She gave some to Adam, and he ate too.
At once they knew they were naked, and shame made them hide. They stitched leaves together to cover themselves.
When God called, Adam blamed Eve, and Eve blamed the serpent. Their trust had broken, and their choice had brought sin into the garden.
God told the serpent that it would be cursed. The woman's offspring would strike its head, though the serpent would strike his heel.
God told Eve that bringing children would bring pain, and told Adam that the ground would resist his work. Their lives would now carry sorrow and toil.
God made garments for Adam and Eve and clothed them. Then he sent them out of Eden, so they could not take fruit from the tree of life.
Cherubim and a flaming sword guarded the way to the tree of life. Adam and Eve could not go back.
Outside Eden, Adam and Eve worked hard for food among thorns. They would grow old and return to the dust from which Adam had been made.
The loss was real, but God had not stopped seeing them. Their story showed how disobedience wounds, and why people need God's rescue.
Eden was behind them, yet God's word about the serpent carried a promise of victory. The Bible keeps that hope as its story continues.
Adam and Eve could not repair what they had broken by themselves. Their first choice reminds us to trust God's good ways and seek his mercy.
God saw that violence and wickedness had spread across the earth. The world he made good was filled with terrible harm.
Noah walked with God. God told him that a great flood was coming, and gave him a way to protect his family and the animals.
God told Noah to build an enormous ark with rooms inside, strong enough to ride the rising water. Noah followed God's instructions.
He covered the ark so water could not enter. It was no little boat; it was a place of shelter for a family and many creatures.
Animals came to Noah, pairs of every kind, and Noah brought them inside. His wife, his sons, and their wives entered too.
Then God shut the door. Rain began to fall, and the ark waited while the world outside changed.
Rain fell for forty days and nights, and the waters rose higher and higher. The ark lifted from the ground and began to float.
The flood covered the land and even the highest mountains. Inside the great ark, Noah's family and the animals waited in the darkness.
At last God sent a wind, and the waters began to fall. The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
Noah sent out a raven and then a dove. When the dove returned with a fresh olive leaf, Noah knew the earth was appearing again.
When the ground was dry, God told Noah to leave the ark. His family came out, and every animal found the open earth again.
People who remained outside the ark were swept away and drowned. The flood was judgement, and the rescued family stepped into a solemn, changed world.
Noah built an altar and worshipped God. God made a covenant with Noah, his family, and every living creature.
God promised that a flood would never again destroy all life on earth. He set a rainbow in the clouds as the sign of his promise.
The rainbow became a bright reminder of God's covenant. Whenever its colours appeared, God remembered his promise, and his people could remember it too.
The flood story holds sorrow, rescue, and a new beginning together. Noah's family carried God's mercy into the world after the waters were gone.
